DarkAgesInternational Catalog

Explore a comprehensive historical catalog of DarkAges, its international editions and related titles. This catalog brings together researched and documented client versions, release dates, major updates and service milestones, utilizing all known official and community sources of archived publisher pages, posts, and other digital assets.

Titles

DarkAges

1 / 14DarkAges — United States: Logo, image 1 of 14

KRU Interactive

Website

1999 - Present

United States

Launched in 1999 by Nexon’s U.S. company under game director Dave Kennerly. The company became independent as KRU Interactive in 2005 and continues to operate DarkAges for an international player community.

Temuair’s five adventuring paths pair cooperative combat with a player society of politics and religious orders. Aislings also shape its culture through storytelling, art, contests and teaching at the community’s college and library.

Legends of Darkness어둠의 전설

1 / 9Legends of Darkness — South Korea: Logo, image 1 of 9

Nexon Korea

Website

1998 - Present

South Korea

Developed and published by Nexon Korea, Legends of Darkness entered commercial service in South Korea on January 3, 1998 and remains actively developed through regular gameplay updates, bug fixes and seasonal events.

Adventure in Mysosia through five starting classes, with class changes and promotions that allow different skill combinations. Group combat emphasizes complementary roles, while guilds compete for control of towns.

Elancia일랜시아

1 / 11Elancia — South Korea: Logo, image 1 of 11

Nexon Korea

Website

1998 - Present

South Korea

Announced in December 1998 as Nexon’s third online game, Elancia was designed as a shared fantasy society blending Eastern-style artwork with Western mythology. Nexon Korea continues to operate the Korean edition.

Abilities provide specialization distinct from ordinary character levels, across warrior, adventurer and merchant roles. Combat sits alongside fishing, cooking, tailoring and jewelry-making, giving players several ways to develop their characters.

Asgard아스가르드

1 / 5Asgard — South Korea: Logo, image 1 of 5

Nexon Korea

Website

2001 - Present

South Korea

Developed by Nexon Korea and originally presented as DarkAges VI – Asgard, this related Windows MMORPG entered public testing in 2001. Commercial service began on February 4, 2003 and remains active in South Korea.

Character growth combines four progression tracks: level, alignment, fame and faith. Players choose good or evil as they advance into the celestial realm, raise guardian pets and compete in guild castle sieges.

DarkAges (SGDA)

1 / 3DarkAges — Singapore: Logo, image 1 of 3

NexonAsia

Website

2000 - 2003

Singapore

NexonAsia introduced its Singapore DarkAges service in 2000, with beta testing in June and paid service beginning on September 30. It operated alongside Singapore’s later Legends of Darkness service; NexonAsia announced a shutdown for the end of June 2003.

Combined cooperative monster hunting and potion brewing with courtship, marriage and an Aisling community. Local events and civic ranks in Suomi and Rucesion formed part of NexonAsia’s service, sharing the social traditions of DarkAges.

Yami闇の伝説

1 / 11Yami — Japan: Logo, image 1 of 11

Nexon Japan

Website

2001 - 2005

Japan

Nexon Japan began beta testing of Yami, its edition localized into Japanese, on April 16, 2001. Commercial service followed on September 4, 2001 and ended on November 30, 2005.

Skill proficiency grew through repeated use, alongside experience-based leveling and later class changes. Guilds could form alliances, declare hostilities and compete for castles in Mysosia, while marriage and lotteries added social activities beyond hunting.

Legends of Darkness (Singapore)

NexonAsia

Website

2002 - 2003

Singapore

Introduced by NexonAsia in December 2002, this separate service localized the Korean Legends of Darkness into English. Its beta ran alongside SGDA; NexonAsia announced the regional services’ shutdown for the end of June 2003.

A localization of the Korean game into English, sharing its fantasy setting and core character professions. Party combat paired fighters and martial artists with rogues, spellcasters and healers whose abilities supported one another.

Legends of Orphelias

1 / 3Legends of Orphelias — NexonAsia: Logo, image 1 of 3

NexonAsia

Website

2001 - 2002

Malaysia

Operated in Malaysia by TIME dotNet in partnership with NexonAsia, Legends of Orphelias entered beta testing in 2001. Its server closed on May 31, 2002 as the service moved to Legends of Temuair.

Preserved community accounts describe a reworking of DarkAges with different maps, professions, skills and spells, open combat between players, and creature companions that grew over time.

Legends of Temuair

1 / 5Legends of Temuair — Malaysia: Logo, image 1 of 5

NexonAsia

Website

2002 - 2004

Malaysia

Available by 2002 through NexonAsia and local operator TIME dotNet in Malaysia as the successor to Legends of Orphelias.

Built on the Temuair edition of DarkAges, combining group adventure with trade, crafting, eight interactive religions and player politics. Players could tailor armour, make weapons and take part in contests within the same virtual society.

真世界 [Zhēn Shìjiè]

1 / 4真世界 — Taiwan: Logo, image 1 of 4

APEXON Technology

Website

2001

Taiwan

Licensed from Nexon and localized by APEXON Technology (捷生資訊), 真世界 was promoted in Taiwan in 2001. Its original website announced client testing in Traditional Chinese for selected participants.

Set in Temuair and localized into Traditional Chinese, with five adventuring professions. Publisher guides described rogues using traps, wizards casting elemental spells and priests conducting weddings.

                        Legend

                        Original

                        Repack
                        Main client or patch files and folders extracted from the original source package and repackaged as a ZIP.

                        Client
                        A client installation, supplied as an installer, a self-extracting archive or packaged game files.
                        Patch
                        An update program that replaces existing game files or modifies them to produce updated files. It requires the stated base client.

                        General Notes

                        DarkAges — United States

                        Section topPage top
                        United States download context
                        SubjectNotesSources
                        Mirror filenames and actual client versions
                        • The 3.73 single-file Installer is also mirrored as DarkAges-3.61.exe, DarkAges_Key_3.71.exe and DarkAges_Key_5.21.exe. Those copies are byte-identical; their names do not establish changed 3.61, 3.71 or 5.21 clients
                        • The recovered genuine 5.21 ZIP contains its own three-part Wise Installer and differs from the mislabeled 5.21 mirror of 3.73
                        • DarkAges-4.52.zip contains the complete original 4.51 multipart Installer. Each ZIP member matches the corresponding official /451/multiple/ volume; the filename does not establish a changed U.S. 4.52 build
                        		[14] [43] [53] [54] [62] [63]
                        3.73 single-file and multipart packaging
                        • The standalone and four-part 3.73 Installers have identical installed-client manifests, despite different executable wrappers and Installer support/script data. They are alternative delivery packages, not byte-identical copies of the same wrapper
                        		[14] [43]

                        Legends of Darkness — South Korea

                        Section topPage top
                        South Korea download context
                        SubjectNotesSources
                        3.11 disc installer variants
                        • The Hitel and Nice discs contain different original Installer wrappers (LodR.exe and Lod.exe), but all 1,204 installed payload files match exactly, including Legend.exe
                        		[30] [31]

                        DarkAges — Singapore

                        Section topPage top
                        Singapore download context
                        SubjectNotesSources
                        3.51 help-file variants
                        • The two Singapore 3.51 packages contain the same game executable and differ only in DarkAges.dat, whose changed member is crehlp.txt. One package has Singapore-customized help; the other has U.S.-matching help and a DarkAges.dat byte-identical to U.S. 3.51
                        		Research notes
                        4.21 executable and packaged patch
                        • The standalone darkages.exe and the replacement executable inside dapatch.exe are byte-identical. This is an executable-only update; a required starting version, including a route from 3.51, remains unverified
                        		[45]

The archive adds Legend.cfg and Legends.prf and omits music/5.mus through music/9.mus. Its independently distinct Orphelias identity remains unconfirmed

                        Verification

                        File Verification Methodology

                        Verification considers file identity and historical provenance separately. SHA-256 fingerprints the retrieved bytes and reveals identical copies under different filenames. A hash alone cannot establish publisher origin: that attribution depends on the original distribution route, archived official links and corroborating records.

                        Downloads are checked for completeness and actual contents, including error pages and partial installers. Extracted packages are compared across all members: executables, data, configuration, documentation and music. Installer labels, version files, executable version metadata and embedded regional markers are read together; patch instructions help identify source and target versions. Different installer wrappers can contain matching payloads, while matching executables can accompany different client packages.

                        The researcher must also resist familiar labels and expected conclusions. Mirror filenames are claims to investigate, repeated copies are one witness, and contradictory evidence is sought before accepting an attribution. This has exposed files labeled 3.61 that are actually identical to the recovered 3.73 installer. Publisher news provides historical context, but unresolved discrepancies remain qualified instead of being forced into a tidy chronology.

                        Verification Notes

                        File and package identity

                        The Downloads tables name each retrieved object and describe its contents. Archive and disc-image sizes refer to the containing file. The Hashes section fingerprints only the extracted main game executable; it does not identify its installer, archive or complete client package. Original package identities remain in the Research Notes and preserved catalog records.

                        Archive labels identify external mirrors. Exact-hash copies share a row while keeping all mirror filenames and links. Multipart volumes remain listed together; every required volume is needed for a complete installer. Hosted Download links are placeholders until hosting is configured.

                        Package comparisons include every extracted file: executables, data, text, configuration, music and supporting files. Matching one executable or a version label alone does not establish whole-client equality. Extraction paths and packaging comparisons appear in Research Notes.

                        Regional variants

                        The Singapore 3.51 distributions differ in embedded help text. Temuair and Orphelias-labeled 4.20 packages share core files but differ in configuration and music.

                        No complete client packages have been established as identical across confirmed country editions. Individual files can match across releases: Singapore and U.S. 3.51 share a DarkAges.dat variant; Korean 9.100 production and 9.570 Hades share Legend.dat.

                        Research

                        Methodology

                        The catalog reconstructs the history of each edition from surviving records and software. Publisher announcements, download pages and regional guides provide the starting point. Contemporary reporting from Impress, Vector and 4Gamer helps establish dates and terminology; community histories and preservation mirrors supply leads to check against earlier evidence.

                        Research follows regional names, version numbers, filenames and original download routes. Archived publisher pages and Wayback capture-index queries help recover discontinued links. DiscMaster, magazine CDs and preserved disc images provide clients missing from websites. Current Korean launcher configurations and file manifests have also been examined to distinguish present distribution from historical installers.[40] [296] [297]

                        Each record separates an announced update, client availability, testing, commercial launch and service closure. File timestamps and archive captures help place the evidence in time but do not automatically become release dates. Migrated news dates are checked against events described in the text. Conflicting numbers, incomplete captures and uncertain regional attribution remain visible, with references attached to the claims they support.[298]

                        Research Notes

                        General covers service history and unnumbered releases. Version-specific findings are grouped by title; date-only citations remain indexed in Sources.

                        		[474]
                        Alpha testing — March–April 2001Japan
                        • The publisher closed alpha-monitor recruitment on March 23, 2001 after reaching its intended participant count. This establishes recruitment closure, not the alpha client’s first release date.
                        • An April 11 notice scheduled the alpha edition to end on April 13 at 15:00. It provides no client build number and does not independently confirm completion at that time.
                        		[594] [595]
                        Open beta — April 16, 2001Japan
                        • The April 11 publisher notice announces public beta access from April 16, 2001 at 15:00, explicitly distinguishing it from the limited alpha edition.
                        • A same-day April 16 notice confirms beta downloads resumed after FTP congestion. This corroborates beta distribution that day; neither notice identifies a client version number.
                        		[596] [597]
                        Commercial service — September 4, 2001Japan
                        • The August 6 publisher announcement schedules formal service for September 4. A September 4 notice explicitly confirms formal service began that day and the beta edition ended.
                        • Beta character IDs remained usable. The publisher specifies 1,000 yen per month including tax for up to two characters, with characters below level 10 still free.
                        • These service notices state no client version number. The commercial launch must not be assigned to 4.30 merely because it is the preceding documented numbered update.
                        		[598] [599]
                        5.00 — July 25, 2002 introductionJapan
                        • The July 24 publisher notice schedules the production upgrade from 4.52 for July 25. Its July 25 follow-up explicitly confirms Version 5.00 was introduced, maintenance finished and the full 5.00 client was available.
                        • The February 19, 2003 notice independently identifies 5.00 as the current production client before 5.20. Vector’s earlier package-file date is not an authenticated production introduction date.
                        • The June 25 public test distribution is a separate channel. Matching 5.00 labels do not establish identical test and production binaries; neither package was recovered in this news pass.
                        		[600] [601] [450]
                        5.00 — public test serverJapan
                        • The June 25, 2002 publisher notice explicitly says the 5.00 test server is open to anyone, free of charge, without a NEXON account. Production characters were copied from June 25 data; test changes would not carry back to production.
                        • The publisher advertises Yami500T.exe at 65.3 MB, but these package bytes and size remain unverified. June 27 at 17:00 is the planned test closing time, not a confirmed completed shutdown.
                        • The source calls this a test server rather than explicitly calling it beta. Keep it separate from production 5.00 introduced July 25 and from the June 28 soccer-event schedule.
                        		[602]
                        4.51 / 4.52 — introduction conflictJapan
                        • The January 24, 2002 notice plans a 4.30 to 4.51 upgrade for late January or early February. February 5 and 6 notices instead schedule 4.52 for February 14, still naming 4.30 as current.
                        • A preserved news index lists an unlinked February 14 headline saying the 4.52 patch distribution started; its full announcement body and article URL were not recovered. March 18 instead names 4.51 as current and March 19 confirms 4.52 introduction.
                        • These sources do not establish whether the earlier schedule changed, the service reverted, or a version label was mistaken. The first 4.52 release date remains unknown; February 14 is retained as an earlier scheduled/index-reported date and March 19 as a confirmed introduction. Neither is silently selected as the first release.
                        • The earlier 4.52 announcement lists changes relative to 4.30. Those planned changes are retained in the source record rather than merged into the later 4.51-relative changelog without qualification.
                        		[603] [604] [605] [606] [448] [449]
                        2004 — service and gameplay changesJapan
                        • The June 3, 2004 notice schedules an account-price reduction from 1,000 to 500 yen per month from July 1, retaining two characters per account. This is an announced pricing change, not a newly numbered client.
                        • June 8 completed maintenance confirms accelerated skill-level growth. A later update that day corrects reduced spell-level caps for some classes. Neither notice states a client version number; these changes must not be assigned automatically to 5.22b.
                        		[607] [608] [609]
                        2005 — free access and closure scheduleJapan
                        • The July 1, 2005 publisher notice announces service closure for November 30 and free access beginning September 1. The November 30 date is an explicit shutdown schedule; a same-day completion notice was not recovered.
                        • A September 1 notice confirms fees were set to free at 12:20 that day, with paid-service character data retained and previously unregistered characters allowed to log in. No new client version number is supplied.
                        		[610] [611]
                        Publisher date inconsistenciesJapan
                        • Notice74 prints 2001/02/26 amid surrounding 2002 notices and reports maintenance ended without changes. Preserve that literal header; it does not securely establish a February 2001 service or client milestone.
                        • Noticeold103 prints 2002/04/30 while discussing the June screenshot winner and July voting. The old-news index dates that subject July 1. Neither the parsed header nor the Wayback capture date independently settles its publication day.
                        • The broader archive review includes unnumbered fixes, maintenance, rollback, support changes and recurring events. Their existence is preserved in the full article review and must not be converted into invented client numbers.
                        		[612] [613] [606]
                        Archived news — review coverageJapan
                        • The October 14, 2026 follow-up queried both archived official Japanese hostnames and attempted all 333 observed news HTML paths, ten additional article links and two broken webzine links: 345 targets in total.
                        • The usable captures include 198 article paths representing 154 distinct article texts, plus six index/navigation bodies. Every recovered article was read in full; duplicate copies are one work. The remaining 141 targets have explicit failure records.
                        • This completes the observed linked/archive frontier, not every historical post or every saved revision. A missing body, index headline or capture timestamp must not be presented as a verified release date.

                        • The official introduction says Elancia was announced in December 1998 as Nexon’s third title. An original publisher commercial launch-day notice was not recovered.
                        • The ability guide distinguishes specialization abilities from ordinary levels; it does not establish a level-free game.
                        • This review retains 49 numbered publisher notices and two package-derived executable observations. It is a bounded review, not a complete history.
                        • The December 2024 notice documents later unnumbered client changes, so the 2014 version 5.80 is not a verified final release.
                        • No separate historical patch binary was recovered. A Japanese 3.67 CD report remains a research lead without recovered package bytes or publisher corroboration; community addon versions are not game versions.
                        		[582] [583] [584] [579] [580] [581]
                        6.0.3.0 · Production packageSouth Korea
                        • Production installation payload; embedded PE FileVersion/ProductVersion 6.0.3.0.
                        • Observed from the current official NGM configuration on 14 October 2026 UTC; the game was not launched or updated.
                        • Version is the exact embedded PE executable file version, not an inferred dotted publisher patch label. These observations do not establish a publisher-announced change from two-part patch numbers to four-part public release numbers.
                        • The package was obtained from the official NGM configuration; automatic updates or live-server builds were not checked.
